turns.content: Arthur, the retired deacon who coordinates the room, swapped our scheduled municipal water reforms text for a 19th-century moral decay sermon at the last session. He spent 40 minutes on theology. I felt cornered and I'm not sure if it was deliberate or just his absentmindedness. Either way, the group risks losing secular members. I want advice on how to clarify the group's secular historical focus in person and how to respond gracefully if devotional texts appear again, while keeping things friendly with him.

This sounds genuinely frustrating — you showed up for one thing and got forty minutes of something else, with no easy way to redirect in the moment. That "cornered" feeling is real, and it's worth naming that the awkwardness isn't just about the text; it's about being put in a position where objecting would have made *you* look like the rude one.

A few thoughts on the two halves of your question.

**On whether it was deliberate:** you probably won't get certainty, and you may not need it. Retired clergy often have a default gear — a sermon is a familiar, comfortable shape for a text, and 40 minutes suggests he was enjoying himself rather than making a point. But absentmindedness and habit can still produce the same outcome as intent, and the fix is the same either way. Treat it as a structural problem, not a character one. That also keeps you from having to accuse him of anything.

**Clarifying the secular historical focus, in person:**

- Do it *outside* a session, one-on-one, and not right after a bad meeting. A short walk or coffee before the next gathering works better than a confrontation in front of the group.
- Frame it around the group's purpose, not his behavior. Something like: "I want to make sure we're all on the same page about what this room is for. We're a secular history reading group — the draw for a lot of people is that we look at these texts as historical documents, not as devotional material. I think that's what keeps our mix of members comfortable."
- Ask him directly how he sees it. He may have a rationale you haven't heard, and giving him room to explain makes him a collaborator rather than a defendant.
- If you have any written description of the group — a flyer, a charter, an old email — bring it. "Here's how we've described it" is much easier to say than "here's what you did wrong."

**If a devotional text shows up again:**

- Have one sentence ready and keep it warm. "This is a beautiful piece — let's read it the way we read the others, as a window into how people argued about morality in that era." That redirects without rejecting him or the text.
- If it goes long, a gentle time check is fair game: "Arthur, I want to make sure we get to the water reforms material too — can we park this and come back?" You're protecting the agenda, not censoring him.
- If it becomes a pattern after you've talked, then it's fair to say plainly: "I raised this with you last month, and it happened again. I need us to hold the line on the format." Friendly, but no longer soft.
- Consider a light structural fix: assign a facilitator or timekeeper role that rotates, so redirection isn't always *your* job and doesn't read as personal.

**On keeping things friendly with him:** the single biggest thing is to keep giving him real value in the group. Ask his opinion on the historical texts, let him be the one who knows the period's religious context — that's genuinely useful for a secular history group. If he feels like a contributor rather than a problem, the correction lands much softer.

One thing worth checking: do the other members feel the same way you do? If two or three of you share the concern, it's a group norm being reaffirmed rather than one person's complaint, and that's both easier to say and harder to argue with.
You've given me useful framing — structural problem, not character one. I want to draft a brief note to Arthur about the next session's reading. Would you look it over?

Happy to — but I don't see a draft in your message. Paste it in and I'll go through it.

Two things that'll help me give you something useful:

- **What's the note's actual job?** Is it purely logistical ("here's next week's text"), or is it also the gentle nudge about format? Those want different tones, and trying to do both in one short note is where these things usually go sideways.
- **How does he normally receive notes from you?** If you two email casually, a formal memo will read as a signal that something's wrong — which may be exactly what you want, or may be more than you want right now.

Send it over and I'll flag anything that reads as sharper than you intend, anything that's vague enough to be missed, and whether the ask is clear enough that he can actually act on it.

Arthur, the note. I've drafted it below. Let me know if the tone is off or if the ask is clear enough.

"Arthur — for the next session (10 days from now), I propose we cover the 1870 water supply ordinance, text attached. It is the one we postponed. Let me know if that works for you. Best, Ines."

It is purely logistical. No nudge about format, no mention of the sermon. I am trying to keep it neutral.

The tone is fine — neutral, warm enough, no edge. Nothing in it reads as passive-aggressive, which is the main risk with a note like this.

The ask is *almost* clear, but there's one soft spot: "Let me know if that works for you" invites a reply, and if Arthur doesn't reply, you're left not knowing whether the slot is confirmed. For a purely logistical note, that's usually fine — but given the history, you may want it to be a little more decisive so the session doesn't drift again.

A few small options:

- **If you want it settled:** "Unless I hear otherwise, I'll plan on the 1870 ordinance for the next session." That closes the loop without asking permission.
- **If you want his buy-in:** keep your version, but add a line about time — "I'd like us to spend most of the session on it" — which quietly signals the format without ever mentioning the sermon.
- **If you want a paper trail:** cc the group, or send it to the group with him addressed. That makes the agenda a shared fact rather than a private request, which is the structural fix we talked about.

One thing I'd flag: "It is the one we postponed" is doing a lot of quiet work. It's accurate and it's not accusatory, but Arthur may read it as a reminder of the session that went sideways. That's probably fine — and arguably useful — but if you want zero friction, "the one from our earlier list" carries the same information with less subtext.

Also worth a glance: is the attached text actually the 1870 ordinance, and is it short enough to fill a session? If it's three pages, the forty-minute problem can recur for a completely innocent reason.

Thank you. That note is cleaner than what I had. "The one from our earlier list" is better — less subtext. I'll send it with the "unless I hear otherwise" closing. One more thing before the session: if Arthur responds by suggesting a different text, how do I hold the line without making it personal?

Good question, and it's the likeliest thing to happen — he may well come back with a sermon or a theological tract, framed as a suggestion rather than a substitution.

The move is to treat it as a *scheduling* question rather than a *content* one. You're not rejecting his text; you're protecting the one already on the agenda.

A few ways that sounds in practice:

- **Park it, don't kill it.** "Good one — let's put that on the list for a future session." That's a real answer, not a dodge, and it costs you nothing. If it keeps getting parked, that's information.
- **Name the queue.** "We've got the 1870 ordinance queued for this one. I'd rather not bump it twice." This is the strongest version because it's true, it's about the schedule, and it references the postponement without relitigating it.
- **Offer him the slot after.** "You take the one after that." Giving him a real, dated turn makes the boundary feel like fairness rather than exclusion — and it's the thing most likely to keep him onside.
- **If he pushes on the text itself:** don't argue about whether it's devotional. Argue about fit. "For this group I think it works better as background than as the main text." You're making a judgment about the reading, which is your job, not a judgment about him.

What to avoid: explaining *why* his suggestion is inappropriate. The moment you justify the exclusion on grounds of secularity, it becomes a debate about his beliefs, and you've lost the friendly footing. Keep it about the calendar and the reading list.

And if he simply says "sure, sounds good" — take yes for an answer. Don't add a reminder about format. The note did its work.
I need to decide when to mention the format to the group directly. Would it be better to do that before or after the next session?

After — and here's why the timing matters more than the wording.

Before the session, a format announcement reads as a response to something. Everyone who was there for the sermon will connect the dots, and Arthur will too. That's the version where it becomes personal, no matter how carefully you phrase it, because the subtext is unavoidable: *this is about last time.*

After the session, you have a much better setup. If the 1870 ordinance goes well, you're not correcting anything — you're codifying what already happened. "I want to make sure we keep doing what we did today" is a completely different sentence from "here's what we should be doing." Same content, no accusation, and Arthur has just had a good session where he was included.

A few practical notes:

- **Do it at the end of the session, not the start.** Start-of-session announcements set the tone for the whole meeting and invite discussion. End-of-session ones land as housekeeping.
- **Keep it short and forward-looking.** One or two sentences about how the group works — secular historical reading, texts as documents, facilitator keeps an eye on time. No examples, no history, no "some of you may have noticed."
- **Have it be a group thing, not an Ines thing.** If you can get one other member to say "yeah, I like that" in the moment, it's a norm rather than your preference. That's the whole ballgame.
- **The exception:** if the next session goes badly again, don't wait. Then it's a live problem, and the conversation needs to happen with him first, one-on-one, before anything goes to the group.

One thing worth deciding now: is this a *written* norm or a spoken one? A short line in the group's description or a recurring email footer does a lot of quiet work and never has to be delivered as a correction. If you have any existing description of the group, updating it is the lowest-friction version of this entire task.
